impact_assessment: Customer ticket-detail reads fail with HTTP 500 after a new release. Ticket creation still works, so impact is partial but blocks confirmation of processing and current ticket state.

hypotheses.hypothesis: PostgreSQL outage or missing ticket data
hypotheses.evidence: Database health is HTTP 200 and the affected ticket row exists directly in PostgreSQL during the failure.
Cache and queue health endpoints remain HTTP 200 and readiness reports all dependencies healthy.
The same X-Request-ID reaches the API and the API logs the RuntimeError for the ticket-read handler.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Release-specific application regression in ticket detail read
hypotheses.evidence: Failure appears only on the bad application release; correlated API logs contain the runtime exception, and rollback to the known-good release restores the same ticket read.

actions.action: Compare customer-path failure with readiness and dependency health
actions.reason: A green readiness endpoint does not prove every application route is usable.

actions.action: Create a fresh ticket and verify its row directly in PostgreSQL
actions.reason: This separates an application read regression from data loss or failed persistence.

actions.action: Correlate the failing read through Nginx/API logs, Loki, and Tempo using the edge-owned request ID
actions.reason: Layer-specific evidence is required before changing infrastructure or escalating application code.

actions.action: Compare the failing release with the known-good release and roll back the simulated environment
actions.reason: Customer restoration is safer and faster than live code editing when a release-specific regression is proven.

actions.action: Re-test the original ticket and then run the complete release/customer verification
actions.reason: Recovery requires proving both the reported symptom and the broader customer journey are restored.

current_assessment: APP-001 is resolved operationally by rollback. Evidence isolates the defect to ticket-read application code in the bad release while dependencies and persisted data remain healthy. Permanent code correction belongs to development/L3; L2 should retain the request ID, bad version, reproduction, logs/traces, and rollback evidence.
